title: Metallic bonding

draft.title: Metallic bonding
card: A metal is a lattice of positive metal ions. Each atom has given up its outer electrons, and these electrons are free to move through the whole structure.
The free electrons are called delocalised electrons. They form a sea around the ions. The attraction between the positive ions and this sea of electrons is the metallic bond.
Metals conduct electricity because the delocalised electrons can move through the metal as a current when a voltage is applied.
Metals can be bent and shaped because layers of ions can slide past each other. The sea of electrons moves with them and keeps holding the ions together, so the metal does not shatter.
draft.remember: Metal ions sit in a sea of moving electrons, which carry charge and let the layers slide.

a.q: Why can a copper wire carry an electric current?
opts: Delocalised electrons can move through the lattice
Positive ions move freely along the wire
Electrons are shared in fixed pairs between atoms
Copper atoms gain electrons to form negative ions
a.why: The delocalised electrons are free to move, so they carry charge through the metal. The ions stay in the lattice and do not flow along the wire. Electrons in fixed pairs would not be free to move.
a.clue: Which particles are free to move in a metal?

b.q: Mia hits a thin sheet of aluminium with a hammer and it changes shape without breaking. Which statement best explains this?
opts: Layers of ions slide while the electron sea holds them
The layers of ions repel each other and push apart
The delocalised electrons are removed by the hammer
Each ion is bonded to just one neighbouring ion
b.why: When the layers of ions slide, the delocalised electrons move with them and keep attracting the ions, so the bond is not broken. Repulsion between layers would make the metal break apart, which is what the tempting option wrongly suggests.
b.clue: What keeps holding the ions together as the layers move?

a.best: Delocalised electrons can move through the lattice

b.best: Layers of ions slide while the electron sea holds them
